course.title: How Computers Solve Problems
course.description: Write down a procedure precisely enough that something without judgement could follow it, then work out how long it would take.
course.audience: Someone who uses computers daily and wants to understand how a program decides what to do, without learning a language first.

paragraphs: A computer does exactly what its instructions say, in the order they are written: it has no judgement with which to fill in what the writer left out, and it cannot ask what was meant. A program is therefore a list of steps written precisely enough to be followed on those terms, and computer science begins from that fact, because so much of what a computer does, from keeping a contact list in order to finding a route, has to be written out as such steps before the machine can do any of it.

Two questions can be put to any such list of steps, and both can be answered on paper. What the steps do is settled by following them one at a time and noting what each one leaves behind for the next, which tells you what a program will produce before it is run. How long they take is settled by counting them, and a count belongs to the method and the input whichever computer runs it, so two methods can be compared fairly without timing either. Searching an unordered list of a million numbers may mean looking at every one, whereas a sorted list of the same length can be searched with at most twenty comparisons, and a difference of that size shows up in the counts before either search is run.
You do not need to know a programming language, because the programs are a few lines of Python-style code and each lesson explains a line before it asks you to follow it.
outcomes: You'll be able to follow a short program line by line and say what x holds at the end.
You'll be able to say which branch of an if/else runs, including when a value sits exactly on the edge of the test.
You'll be able to count how many times a loop runs and spot one that will never stop.
You'll be able to count the checks a linear search and a binary search make on a list.
You'll be able to say how the number of checks grows with the length of the list, and when a sorted list is worth having.

lessons.title: Steps a machine could follow

lead.text: The card in the opening worked because every line on it could be carried out without making a decision. A machine cannot choose at all, so a procedure written for one has to be made of steps that each mean *one* thing.

A procedure that meets this standard is called an **algorithm**: a list of steps, each of them exact, that comes to an end and leaves an answer. The word is a Latin form of the name of al-Khwarizmi, a mathematician working in Baghdad in the ninth century, whose book on arithmetic with the Hindu-Arabic numerals reached Europe in Latin translation.

afterFigure.text: The other two conditions in the definition, that the list is *finite* and that it ends with an answer, are what make sure the machine eventually stops and has produced something. A list that meets all three conditions can be followed by anyone, or anything, **without having to understand what the writer meant**.

reveal.text: A program does the same thing, with one difference: the number being carried along is given a name, and the next screen introduces it.

lead.text: On the card, the running number was something you held in your head. A program cannot hold anything in its head, so it keeps the number in a named place called a **variable**, and the name used throughout this course is `x`. The line `x = 3` puts the number 3 into `x`, and a line that stores a value in this way is called an **assignment**.
The equals sign in an assignment does not state that two things are equal, as it does in algebra. It is an instruction to *store*, and whatever stands on its right is worked out first.

afterFigure.text: That is why the second line, `x = x + 2`, is perfectly ordinary. Read as algebra it would claim that a number equals itself plus 2, which is impossible. Read as an assignment it says: take the value `x` holds now, which is 3, add 2 to make 5, and store 5 in `x`. The 3 is gone, because a variable holds **one value at a time**, and storing a new value *replaces* the old one.
Run the code in the figure and step through it with the trace control to watch x change from line to line.

lead.text: A program of several lines is followed the way the card was: from the top line to the bottom, one line at a time, with each [[assignment|A line such as x = 3 that stores a value in x. Met earlier in this lesson.]] working on the value that the line before it stored. Following a program in this way and writing down x after every line is called **tracing** it, and it is the main way to find out what a program does without running it.

afterFigure.text: Each line sees only the value that the one before it stored, never one that `x` held earlier, which is why the *order* of the lines is part of what the program means.

reveal.text: Run the code above and step through it to compare: x reads 3, then 5, then 20 after the three lines.

lead.text: The program below uses two operations, doubling and adding 1, and starts from 5. Doubling gives 10, and adding 1 to that gives 11, as [[tracing|Following a program line by line and noting x after each one. Met earlier in this lesson.]] the program shows. Had the two lines been written the other way round, adding 1 would have given 6 and doubling would then have given 12, so the same two instructions make a *different* program when their order changes.

afterFigure.text: The reason is that the second line does not receive the original 5. It receives whatever the first line stored, and exchanging the lines therefore changes what each of them works on. What can never be assumed is that the order **does not matter**.

workedSteps.text: Line 1 stores 3 in x.
Line 2 multiplies the stored 3 by 4 and stores the product.
Line 3 adds 2 to the value that line 2 stored.

lead.text: In the program below, the second line is `x = 1`. It makes no use of the 9 that `x` held: it simply stores 1 in the [[variable|A named place that holds one value at a time. Met earlier in this lesson.]], and the 9 is gone.

afterFigure.text: A line that mentions `x` on its right-hand side, such as `x = x + 5`, *builds on* the old value, while a line that does not, such as `x = 1`, **discards it**. Looking for a line of the second kind is the quickest way to shorten a trace, because everything above it stops mattering.

workedSteps.text: Line 1 stores 2 in x.
Line 2 adds 3 to the stored 2.
Line 3 multiplies whatever x holds now, which is 5.
No lines remain, so x finishes at 15.

reveal.text: The 7 was discarded the moment line 2 stored 2, so a trace could have started at line 2 and given the same result.
Tracing the repaired program gives 4, then 6, then 18, whereas the broken version would have finished at 9, so the repair changes the result a great deal.

blocks.text: Here is a card with three instructions on it: start with 8, add 4, halve what you have. Anyone can follow it and finish with 6, because each instruction names an exact operation and applies to **whatever you are holding at that moment**.

A computer program is a card of this kind, written for a machine that cannot ask what was meant, so it does *exactly* what the lines say, in the order they are written. That is what lets you work out what a program does without running it, by following its lines one at a time.

lessons.title: Choosing between paths

lead.text: The till rule becomes a program once the bill is replaced by `x`. In the figure the first line stores 8 in `x`, and the line `if x > 5:` is the test. It asks whether `x` is greater than 5, a question that can be answered only by *true* or *false*, and a test of this kind is called a **condition**.

The lines beneath it are indented by four spaces, and the indentation is what marks them as belonging to the test. The indented lines straight after the `if` line form one **branch**, which runs only when the condition is true. The line `else:` begins the other branch, which runs only when the condition is false, so *exactly one* of the two branches runs each time and the other is skipped.

afterFigure.text: Here `x` holds 8, and `8 > 5` is true, so the first branch runs and `x` becomes 18. Had `x` held 3 instead, the condition would have been false, the `else` branch would have run, and `x` would have become 2. Run the code and step through it with the trace control to see the test line appear as a step of its own before either branch begins.

reveal.text: A program has to make the same choice, and the next screen shows how it says which of the two readings it means.
Run the code above to compare: the test line appears once in the trace, and a single assignment follows it.

lead.text: Every test of this kind has a place where its answer changes. For `x > 5` that place is 5, and the symbol `>` means *strictly* greater, so 5 itself fails the test, exactly as a bill of £30 fails “over £30”. Writing `>=` instead, which is read as “greater than or equal to”, makes 5 pass. A value that sits exactly where a test changes its answer is called a **boundary value**.

afterFigure.text: The two tests agree about every other value: 3 and 4 fail both of them, and 6 and 7 pass both. **They differ only at the boundary value**, which is why it is the value most worth checking when you follow a program. The symbol `<` is the mirror image of `>`, meaning “less than” and again leaving out equality, and `<=` is the mirror image of `>=`.

Line 2 is the test, and it is worked out with the value now stored in x.
The condition is true, so the first branch runs and the else branch is skipped.
No lines remain, so x finishes at 14.

steps.headline: Change the test in the earlier program to `x >= 5`, and trace it again from `x = 5`.

workedSteps.text: Line 1 stores 5 in x, as before.
Line 2 is the test, now written `x >= 5`, and it is worked out with the stored value.
The test decides which branch runs, and that branch then changes x.

lead.text: A line that is not indented, and so sits after the `else` branch, belongs to neither branch: it runs whichever path was taken, as soon as the chosen branch has finished. In the program below `7 >= 5` is true, the first branch makes `x` equal to 3, and the final line doubles it to 6.

afterFigure.text: Move the last line four spaces to the right, so that it sits under else, and it would run only when the test was false, whereas left where it is it runs every time.

reveal.text: Had x started at 5, the first branch would have run instead, and the same final line would then have turned 15 into 30.
The broken version finished at 1, because `3 > 3` is false and the `else` branch ran. Testing the boundary value first is the quickest way to find a fault of this kind.

blocks.text: A till program has to apply a rule such as this one: take £4 off any bill over £30, and add the tip afterwards. The program has to put a question about the bill first, and let **the answer decide which path to follow**.
Whichever path a bill takes, it comes back to the same last step, the tip, which is added to every bill, so the rule splits the work into two paths and then joins them again.

lessons.title: Doing it again

lead.text: A set of lines that a program runs again and again is called a **loop**, and each run through those lines is called a **pass**, or an **iteration** in the vocabulary of programming. What makes a loop useful, and what makes it safe, is a test made before *every* pass: if the test is true the lines run once more, and if it is false the loop ends and the program moves on to whatever follows it.

afterFigure.text: Two passes have run and the loop ends with `x` equal to 5, **without the program ever having been told that two passes were needed**: the count follows from the test and from what the lines do to `x`.

A box beside it shows what x holds and how many passes have run: 9 and 0 at the start, 7 and 1 after the first pass, and 5 and 2 after the second, when the test fails.

reveal.text: A program does the same: it repeats one action and checks the rule before each go.

lead.text: The loop in the opening is written with the word `while`. The line `while x > 5:` carries the test, and the lines indented beneath it, which are the lines that get repeated, are called the **body**. A loop written in this way is called a **while loop**, and it reads almost as English does: while `x` is greater than 5, run the body.

The test is made before the first pass as well as before every later one, and that has a consequence that is easy to overlook. If the [[condition|A test with a true or false answer. Met in 'Choosing between paths'.]] is false when the loop is first reached, the body does not run at all.

afterFigure.text: In the program in the figure the body is the single line `x = x - 5`. The test `20 > 12` is true, so `x` becomes 15; `15 > 12` is true, so `x` becomes 10; and `10 > 12` is false, so the loop ends. The test was made three times and the body ran only twice, because **the last test is the one that fails**, and a failed test never runs the body. Counting passes therefore means counting the tests that came out true, and you can check it by looking for the three Test steps in the trace.

reveal.text: Run the code above to compare: the trace shows the Test step four times and the body three times, because the last test is the one that fails.

workedSteps.text: Line 1 stores 10 in x.
The test is made first, with the stored value, and it is true, so the body runs.
The test is made again, and the body runs for a second time.
The test is made once more, and the body runs for a third time, which brings x to the boundary value of the test.
The test is made with x equal to 4, and it is false, so the body is not run again.
The loop made three passes and ends with x equal to 4.

reveal.text: Nothing in the body ran, so `x` is still 0, the value it started with.

lead.text: A while loop decides after every pass whether to continue, but sometimes the number of passes is known before the program starts, and a **for loop** states it directly. In the line `for i in range(3):` the expression `range(3)` produces the three values 0, 1 and 2, and the body runs once for each of them, so it runs *three* times. The name `i` holds the value belonging to the current pass, but the bodies in this course never use it, so the line can be read as “repeat three times”.

afterFigure.text: The range always stops one short of the number in the brackets, so `range(4)` gives 0, 1, 2 and 3, and **the number in the brackets is the number of passes**.

reveal.text: `range(4)` gives 0, 1, 2 and 3, and the body ran for each of them, so `x` went from 1 to 3, then 5, then 7, then 9.

lead.text: Nothing outside a while loop stops it. It ends only because its body has changed `x` until the test comes out false, and the program below shows the usual arrangement. The test `x < 20` is made with `x` equal to 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18, each time the body adds 3, and `x` reaches 21, where the test fails.

afterFigure.text: Now suppose that the body subtracted 3 instead. Then `x` would go 3, 0, −3 and on downwards, always below 20, so the test would never become false and the loop would never end. A loop of this kind is called an **infinite loop**, and it is one of the commonest faults in programs because every line of it looks reasonable by itself. **The body has to move x towards the point where the test fails.** Change the `+` in the figure's code to a minus sign and run it: the trace stops after 100 steps and says why, which a real machine would not do.

reveal.text: With the original body, x would have grown 4, 5, 6 and on without end, and the test would have stayed true for ever.

lessons.orientation: Count how many times a loop runs, and see what makes it stop.

blocks.text: Here is a program of three lines. The first stores 9 in `x`, the second begins with the word `while` and reads `while x > 5`, and the third, `x = x - 2`, is indented beneath it.
Repetition is what lets a program deal with work whose amount is not known when the program is written, and a repeated test **lets the machine settle the count while the program runs**.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count how many times a loop runs and spot one that will never stop.

recap.keyIdea: A loop runs its body for as long as its test is true, so the number of passes is the number of true tests, and the body has to move x towards the point where the test fails.

blocks.text: You counted passes in a while loop by listing the value of `x` at the start of each one, and saw that a loop whose test is false at the start never runs at all. A for loop with `range(n)` makes *n* passes, and a while loop whose body moves `x` the wrong way never ends.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses a loop for the commonest job in programming, looking through a list for one item, and counts how many checks it takes.

lessons.title: Looking things up

lead.text: The search described in the opening has a name: it is called a **linear search**. It starts at the first item and compares it with the value being looked for, which is called the **target**, and if the two differ it moves on to the next item and compares again.

Each comparison of an item with the target is a **check**, and the search ends at the first check that matches or after the last item has been checked without a match. Those are the only two ways it can end, so counting the checks is a fair way to measure how much work a search has done.

afterFigure.text: Press Start search and then Next check to step through it, and try other targets such as 7 or 4 to see how the number of checks changes.

lead.text: A list keeps its items in order, and a program refers to an item by its position. The position is given as an **index**, and indexes begin at *zero*: the first item has index 0, the second has index 1, and the fifth has index 4.

Starting from zero is the convention of most programming languages, and it is the cause of a very common confusion, between where an item is and how many [[checks|Comparisons of an item with the target. Met earlier in this lesson.]] it took to reach it.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the target is 14, which sits at index 1. The search checks the item at index 0, which is 6, and then the item at index 1, which is 14, so it makes two checks. A search that finds its target at index i has made **i + 1 checks**, because the first check is the item at index 0. The index says where the item is and the number of checks says how much work was done, and the two differ by one.

reveal.text: The 6 sits at index 3, so the number of checks is one more than that, as the previous screen said it would be.

steps.headline: Search the list 4, 9, 1, 6, 2 for the target 1.

workedSteps.text: The search begins at index 0, and the first check compares the item there with the target.
The items differ, so the search moves on to index 1.
The third check is at index 2, and the item there matches, so the search stops.
The search made three checks to reach an item whose index is 2.

reveal.text: The 8 sits at index 0, so the search stops at the first item it compares. The index is one less than the number of checks.

lead.text: So far every target was somewhere in the list. If it is not, the search has no match to stop at, and it can reach its answer only by running out of items. In a list with no order there is no way to skip any of them, because the last item could hold the target, so the search has to check *every* item before it can say that the target is missing.

afterFigure.text: **A missing target costs a check for every item in the list.**

reveal.text: The search made five checks and found no 7, which cost exactly as much as a search for a target in last place would have.
The pile behaves exactly like a list of nine items in no order, so when your paper is last, or not there at all, you turn over all nine.

lead.text: The fewest is one check, when the target is the first item, and this is called the **best case**. The most is one check for every item, when the target is last or missing, and this is called the **worst case**.

afterFigure.text: Every other position gives a count between them, and a list of n items needs at most n checks, so the worst case for 50 items is 50. The worst case is the one a program has to be ready for, because it is the count that no target can exceed: **the checks can never be more than the length of the list**.

blocks.text: Take a program that holds the five numbers 5, 12, 7, 9 and 3 in a **list**, a row of values each stored in its own place, and has to find out whether 12 is among them. The numbers are in no particular order, so nothing about 5 tells the program where 12 might be, and the only way to be sure is to *look*, one place at a time, until 12 turns up or the places run out.
How many looks a search needs depends on the list and on where the value happens to sit, and that count is what the search **costs**.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count the checks a linear search makes on a list, including when the target is last or missing.

recap.keyIdea: A linear search checks items in order, so a target at index i costs i + 1 checks and a missing target costs one check for every item.

blocks.text: You counted the checks a linear search makes when the target was first, last and missing, and found that the worst case is a check on every item, so the count can never exceed the length of the list. You also kept apart an item's *index*, which starts at 0, and the number of checks made to reach it, which is one more.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson shows that a sorted list lets a search skip items, which makes its worst case far smaller.

lessons.title: Halving the problem

reveal.text: A search that makes use of the order can discard whole blocks at a time, and the next screen turns this into a method.

lead.text: A list whose items run from smallest to largest is called **sorted**, and a sorted list allows a search that is far quicker than checking every item. The search is called **binary search**, and each of its steps is one **comparison** of the target with the middle item of the range that is still possible, which at the start is the whole list. A comparison is what the last lesson called a check.

There are three outcomes. If the middle item is the target, the search ends. If it is smaller than the target, then it and everything before it are too small and can be discarded. If it is larger, then it and everything after it are too large and can be discarded. In the last two cases the search repeats on the items that remain.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the target is 31 and the list has seven items. The middle item is 18, at [[index|A position in a list, counted from 0. Met in 'Looking things up'.]] 3, which is smaller than 31, so 18 and the three items before it are discarded. The remaining items are 24, 31 and 40, whose middle is 31, and the second comparison finds the target. The search made *two* comparisons, where a linear search would have made six. When the range has an even number of items there are two middle items, and this course always takes the lower one, so that every search can be followed exactly.

lead.text: Take the list 9, 2, 7, 4, 6, which is not in order, and search it for 9. The middle item is 7, which is smaller than 9. In a sorted list that would mean that everything before the 7 is smaller still, and so the search could discard it, but here the 9 stands *before* the 7 and would be thrown away with the left half. The search would then report that 9 is missing, which is wrong.

afterFigure.text: Sorting is therefore the price of the method, and it has to be paid first. **Without the order, binary search gives wrong answers**, and not merely slow ones, because discarding half the list is justified only when every discarded item is known to be on the wrong side of the target.

steps.headline: Search the sorted list 1, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 for the target 12.

workedSteps.text: The whole list is possible, and its middle item is 9, at index 3. The target is compared with it.
The 9 and the items before it are discarded, leaving 12, 15 and 18. The middle of those is 15, which is compared next.
The 15 and the item after it are discarded, leaving only 12, which is compared and matches.
The search made three comparisons, with 9, then 15, then 12.

reveal.text: The middle of the seven items is the one at index 3, which holds 11, so the very first comparison meets the target.
The comparisons were with 11, then 5, then 8, and after the last of them nothing was left, so 10 is missing.

lead.text: A target that is not in the list never produces a match, so the search keeps discarding until nothing remains, and an empty range is its signal that the target is missing.

afterFigure.text: Each comparison discards the middle item and one whole side, so at most half of the other items remain: seven items become at most three, then at most one, then none. A list of seven therefore needs **at most three comparisons**, however the target is placed.

blocks.text: Take the ten items 10, 20, 30 and so on up to 100, written in order from smallest to largest, and suppose that a program compares its target with 40 and finds that the target is larger. Every item before 40 is smaller than 40, and so smaller than the target, which means that **one comparison has ruled out four items at once**, with 40 itself among them, and six items remain.

A list in no order offers nothing like this, because there a failed check says only that one item is not the target and says nothing about any other, which is why a list of a million items can cost a million checks.

recap.keyIdea: Binary search compares the target with the middle of a sorted list and discards the half that cannot hold it, so every comparison removes at least half of what remains.

blocks.text: You found that a sorted list lets one comparison rule out a whole block of items, and counted 2, 1, 3 and 4 comparisons for targets in lists of seven and eight items. You also saw that the order is *essential*: on a list in no order the same method can throw away the target itself.

lessons.title: When the input grows

reveal.text: The target was in last place, so the search had to compare it with every item, and the count equals the length of the list.

lead.text: The obvious way to compare two programs is to time them, but a time depends on the machine, on what else it is doing and on how the program was written, so a time measured on one computer says little about another. The number of comparisons does not change from machine to machine.

The length of the list is called the **input size**, and the question to ask of any method is how its count of comparisons changes as the input size changes. A [[linear search|Checking the items of a list in order until the target is found. Met in 'Looking things up'.]] is the simple case: in the worst case it checks every item, so its count *equals* the input size, and a list twice as long can need twice as many comparisons.
[[Binary search|Comparing with the middle of a sorted range and discarding the half that cannot hold the target. Met in 'Halving the problem'.]] uses the order that a linear search ignores.

afterFigure.text: Whichever side the target is on, a comparison removes the middle item and one whole side, and a side holds half of the other items, so seven items become at most three, and then at most one. **Each comparison at most halves what is left**, which is the whole reason that binary search is quick.

steps.headline: Count the comparisons that binary search can need for 31 sorted items.

workedSteps.text: The search starts with all 31 items, and the first comparison is with the middle item.
After that comparison the target can still be in only part of the list.
The second comparison treats 15 items in the same way: the middle goes and the other 14 split into two sides of 7.
Seven items become at most three, since the other six split into two sides of 3.
Three items become at most one, since the other two split into two sides of 1.
The last item is compared, and then nothing remains. Each of the ranges of 31, 15, 7, 3 and 1 items needed one comparison.

steps.headline: Search the sorted list 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 for the target 13, using binary search.

workedSteps.text: The first comparison is with the middle item, 7, which is smaller than 13, so 7 and the three items before it are discarded.
Carry on with 9, 11 and 13, taking the middle each time.

reveal.text: The target 15 in the figure shows such a case: it was found on the fourth comparison, after 8, 12 and 14.

lead.text: A sorted list of 7 items needs at most 3 comparisons, one of 15 needs 4, one of 31 needs 5, and so on, because each extra comparison allows the list to be about twice as long. The longest lists that 1, 2, 3 and 4 comparisons can handle are 1, 3, 7 and 15 items, and each is double the one before it, plus one.

How the count rises as the input size rises is called the **growth** of a method. The growth of linear search is steep, because its count rises as fast as the list does, whereas the growth of binary search is very gentle.

afterFigure.text: The lengths 7, 15, 31, 63 and 127 are each one less than a power of two, which is why they suit the pattern, and the figure shows linear search needing 127 comparisons where binary search needs 7. **Doubling the list adds one comparison to a binary search**, however long the list already is, whereas it doubles the comparisons of a linear search.

The limits run 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, 127, 255, 511 and 1023, which is ten of them, whereas a linear search of the same list could need all 1023 comparisons.

lead.text: Binary search needs a [[sorted|A list whose items run from smallest to largest. Met in 'Halving the problem'.]] list, so a list in no order has to be sorted first, and sorting is work of its own. Sorting a thousand items takes on the order of ten thousand steps, which is far more than the thousand comparisons that a single linear search can cost. Taken once, therefore, the sort is a poor bargain: sorting and then searching costs 10,010 steps, against at most 1,000 for a linear search.

afterFigure.text: The sort has to be paid for only once, however. After it, each search costs at most ten comparisons and not a thousand, so for 100 searches the plan that sorts first costs 10,000 + 1,000 = 11,000 steps, against 100,000 for a linear search every time. **Sorting pays when the list is searched many times, or when it is kept sorted anyway**, and it does not pay for a single search.

lessons.orientation: Count how many comparisons each search needs as a list grows, and say when binary search is worth its sorting.
lessons.nextAction: Try the changed cases in your review queue.

blocks.text: On a list of seven items a linear search and a binary search both finish so quickly that a program could use either without anyone noticing. The difference appears as the list grows: in the worst case a list of 63 items costs a linear search 63 comparisons and a binary search 6, and the gap keeps widening each time the list doubles. What matters when choosing between the two methods is therefore **how the work rises as the list gets longer**.
Binary search also needs the list to be sorted, and sorting is work in its own right, so there is a point at which the saving from searching begins to outweigh the cost of preparing the list.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say how the number of comparisons grows with the length of the list, and when a sorted list is worth having.

recap.keyIdea: Doubling a list doubles the work of a linear search but adds only one comparison to a binary search, and the sorting that binary search needs pays for itself only over many searches.

blocks.text: You counted at most 3 comparisons for 7 items, 4 for 15, 5 for 31 and 10 for 1023, and saw that each is the number of times a list can be halved before nothing is left. You also set the cost of sorting a list of a thousand items against the cost of searching it, and found that sorting *first* wins once there are enough searches.

questions.prompt: Follow the three lines in order. What is x when the program ends?
hints: Follow the program from top to bottom, one line at a time.
Start at 3, apply the addition, then apply the multiplication to the updated value.
Do not apply both operations to the original 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Starting at 3, adding 2 gives 5, then multiplying by 4 gives 20.

questions.onCorrect: Each line works on the value the line above left in x: 3, then 5, then 20.

misconceptions.feedback: That is x after line 2. Line 3 still has to run.
That multiplies first and adds second. Run the lines top to bottom, as written.
Line 3 multiplies what line 2 stored, not the original 3.

questions.prompt: What is x once line 3 has run?
hints: The multiplication now runs before the addition.
Line 2 has already stored 12.
Add 2 to that stored value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Multiplying 3 by 4 gives 12, then adding 2 gives 14.

questions.onCorrect: The same two instructions in the other order give a different answer, because each works on the value before it.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 2 first, then multiplies. In this program the multiplication runs first.
That multiplies by 4 + 2. Line 3 adds 2 to the value line 2 stored.
That is x after line 2. Line 3 still has to add 2.

questions.prompt: Run the three lines. What is x at the end?
hints: An assignment replaces the old value of x.
The line `x = 2` overwrites the earlier 7.
Apply the final doubling to the newly stored value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second line replaces 7 with 2, and doubling 2 gives 4.

questions.onCorrect: The second line replaced 7 with 2, so only 2 reaches the doubling.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the 7. Line 2 replaced it before line 3 ran.
Line 2 stores 2. It does not add 2 to the 7.
That is x after line 2. Line 3 still has to run.

questions.prompt: A program is meant to start with `x = 4`, add 2 and then triple the result, but its last line adds 3 instead. Once the last line is mended so that it triples `x`, what does the program finish with?
hints: Use the plan described in the question.
Start at 4, add 2, then multiply the updated value by 3.
Trace the repaired program, not the broken one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The repaired program gives (4 + 2) × 3 = 18.

questions.onCorrect: Tracing the repaired program shows the plan working: add 2 first, then triple the result.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the broken version, which adds 3 to the updated x. The repair multiplies.
That triples first and adds 2 second. The plan adds 2 first.
That triples the 4 and skips the add. The plan adds 2 first.

questions.prompt: Trace `x = 5`, then `x = x - 2`, then `x = x * 3`. What is the final `x`?
hints: Each assignment uses the value stored by the line before it.
First reduce 5 by 2.
Multiply that new value by 3.
questions.onCorrect: Each line works on the value the one before left: 5, then 3, then 9.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies before subtracting. Run the lines top to bottom.
That is x after line 2. Line 3 still has to run.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an instruction a machine could carry out as it stands?
hints: A machine cannot decide what “nicer” or “a bit” means. Which line says exactly what to do?
Look for a line that names an operation and an amount.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: x = x + 1

choices.label: Make x nicer
Increase x a bit

questions.onCorrect: `x = x + 1` is exact: it reads the current `x`, adds 1 and stores the result.

misconceptions.feedback: “Nicer” names no operation a machine could perform. It needs an exact change to x.
“A bit” is not an amount. A machine needs the exact change to make.

questions.prompt: Run the program. What is x at the end?
hints: Work out `5 > 5` before running either branch.
A strict greater-than comparison does not include equality.
Follow only the else branch when the condition is false.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: `5 > 5` is false, so the `else` branch subtracts 1: 5 − 1 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: The test `5 > 5` is false, so only the `else` branch runs and the `if` branch is skipped.

misconceptions.feedback: That runs the `if` branch. Check `5 > 5` first: is 5 greater than 5?
That is only the amount the if branch adds, and it would not run here.
One of the two branches always changes x. Which one runs?

questions.prompt: What is x at the end?
hints: The inclusive comparison is `>=` rather than `>`.
Test whether the stored 5 meets that condition.
Run the +10 branch only if the condition is true.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: `5 >= 5` is true, so `x` becomes 5 + 10 = 15.

questions.onCorrect: With `>=` the boundary value takes the `if` branch, so one changed symbol changes the outcome.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the else branch. Is 5 greater than or equal to 5?
That is only the amount added. The if branch adds it to x.

questions.prompt: Run the program. What is x at the end?
hints: Run one branch, then continue after the if/else block.
For this input the else branch subtracts 1.
The later doubling still runs after the chosen branch.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The else branch changes 2 to 1, then the final line doubles it to 2.

questions.onCorrect: The else branch made 1, and the last line runs on both paths, so it doubled that.

misconceptions.feedback: That is x after the branch. The last line still doubles it.
That runs the if branch. Does the starting value reach the threshold?

questions.prompt: A program is meant to add 10 when `x` is at least 3 and to subtract 2 otherwise, but its test is `x > 3`. For the input 3, what should `x` finish as?
hints: The plan says to add 10 when `x` is at least 3. Does 3 count as at least 3?
The broken test `x > 3` leaves 3 out, so it does not follow the plan. Follow the plan instead.
Apply the branch the plan names to the 3 you started with.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Using `x >= 3` takes the first branch and gives 3 + 10 = 13.

questions.onCorrect: At the boundary, `>=` takes the `if` branch and adds 10. Test the exact threshold value first.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the broken version: `3 > 3` is false, so it subtracts 2.
That is only the amount the if branch adds. It adds it to x.

questions.prompt: Which of these tests is true when x is 4?
hints: Each symbol either includes the boundary value or leaves it out.
Substitute 4 for x in each test, and ask whether the symbol allows the two sides to be equal.
questions.onCorrect: With `x` equal to 4, the test `x >= 4` reads `4 >= 4`, which is true because `>=` includes the boundary value. The symbols `>` and `<` both leave it out.

misconceptions.feedback: The symbol `>` means strictly greater, so `4 > 4` is false: equal values fail the test.
The symbol `<` also means strictly, so `4 < 4` is false: equal values fail this test as well.

questions.prompt: A program stores 8 in `x`. If `x < 5` it subtracts 1, and otherwise it divides `x` by 2. What is `x` at the end?
hints: Work out `8 < 5` before changing `x`.
When that test is false, use the otherwise branch.
Divide the current 8 by 2, and do not also subtract 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: `8 < 5` is false, so the other path gives 8 / 2 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: `8 < 5` is false, so the `else` branch halves 8 and the subtraction is skipped.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts 1. Is 8 less than 5?
That runs both branches. Only one runs.

questions.prompt: How many times does the body run?
hints: Check `x > 0` before every pass.
List the values of x at which the body starts, beginning with the initial value in the code.
Do not count the final failed check as a pass.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The body runs for starting values 3, 2 and 1: three passes.

questions.onCorrect: The body runs once for each check that passes. The check that fails ends the loop without a pass.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the check that failed. A failed check does not run the body.
The body also runs when x is 1. List the value of x at the start of each pass.

questions.prompt: A program stores 0 in `x` and then repeats `x = x - 1` while `x > 0`. How many times does the body run?
hints: A while loop makes its test before its first pass.
Compare the initial value with the strict condition before changing it.
If that first test fails, no line of the body runs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first test `0 > 0` is false, so the body runs zero times.

questions.onCorrect: The check comes first, so a loop whose condition starts false never runs its body.

misconceptions.feedback: The body runs only after a check passes, and the first check fails.

questions.prompt: What is x at the end?
hints: The for loop repeats the addition four times.
Each pass adds 2 to the current x, starting from 1.
Add the total increase to the initial value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four additions of 2 take `x` from 1 to 1 + 8 = 9.

questions.onCorrect: A for loop counts its own passes. Four values in the range means four additions of 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 2 only three times. Count the values `range(4)` gives.
That counts five passes. The range stops before 4, so it gives four values.
That is x after one pass. The body runs once for every value in the range.

questions.prompt: A program stores 3 in `x` and then runs `while x > 0` with a body that adds 1 to `x`, so it never ends. If the body subtracts 1 instead, what is `x` when the loop ends?
hints: Trace the repaired subtraction from the given starting value.
The loop continues only while x is positive.
Stop at the first value that makes the displayed test false.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The repaired body takes x through 2, 1 and 0, and then the test is false.

questions.onCorrect: The repaired body moves x towards the failing check, so the loop ends the moment x stops being positive.

misconceptions.feedback: At that value the condition is still true, so the body runs again.
The check comes before the body. Once the condition fails, the body does not run again.

questions.prompt: A program stores 2 in `x`, then repeats `x = x * 2` three times. What is the final `x`?
hints: Apply each doubling to the result of the previous doubling.
The first pass changes 2 to 4.
Perform exactly two more doublings.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three doublings give 4, 8 and 16.

questions.onCorrect: Each pass works on the last result: 4, then 8, then 16.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 2 by 3 once. Each pass doubles the result of the last one.
That is two doublings. The loop runs three times.

questions.prompt: A while loop begins with `x = 5` and runs while `x > 0`. Which change to its body lets the loop stop?
hints: The loop stops only when its condition becomes false.
Choose an update that moves a positive x towards zero.

acceptedIdeas: Subtract 1 each pass
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Subtract 1 each pass

choices.label: Add 1 each pass
Leave x unchanged
Subtract 1 each pass

questions.onCorrect: Subtracting 1 moves `x` towards 0, where `x > 0` fails. A body must move towards the stopping condition.

misconceptions.feedback: Adding 1 moves x further from the stopping point, so the condition stays true.
If x never changes, neither does the check, so the loop never ends.

questions.prompt: Search the list in the figure for 6. How many checks does it take?
hints: Linear search checks values from left to right.
Which items does the search compare before it reaches the one holding the target?
The successful comparison counts as a check too, and the search stops there.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The search checks 8, 3, 11 and 6: four checks.

questions.onCorrect: The search checks 8, 3, 11 and 6, then stops at the match. The matching check counts too.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the index of 6, not the number of checks. Indexes start at 0, while checks are counted from one.
The search stops at the match, so the last item is never checked.

questions.prompt: A linear search looks for 8 in the list in the figure. How many checks does it take?
hints: The search begins with the first item in the list.
Compare that first item with the target.
Count the comparison that finds the match.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first comparison finds 8, so one check is enough.

questions.onCorrect: A target in first place is found by the first check, however long the list is.

misconceptions.feedback: The first index is zero, but the check that finds it still counts as a check.

questions.prompt: Search the list in the figure for 7. How many checks does it take to be sure that 7 is missing?
hints: A list in no order gives no basis for skipping the remaining items.
Continue after each mismatch until the list ends.
Count one check for every item inspected.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All five values must be checked to establish that 7 is missing.

questions.onCorrect: A missing target costs a check for every item, because a list in no order gives nothing to skip by.

misconceptions.feedback: That stops one item early. The last item might hold 7, so it has to be checked.

questions.prompt: Search the eight items in the figure for 6. How many checks does it take?
hints: Find the position of 6 in the displayed eight-item list.
A linear search must inspect all earlier items first.
Count positions starting at one for the number of checks.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The target is last, so all eight values are checked.

questions.onCorrect: A last-place target costs a check for every item, the same as a missing target.

misconceptions.feedback: The target is last, so the final check is the one that finds it. Count it.
That is the value of the target, not the number of checks.

questions.prompt: What is the most checks a linear search can make on a list of 50 items?
hints: The target might be last or missing.
In either case a linear search cannot stop before inspecting the last item.
Use one check per item in the stated list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The target can be last or missing, requiring all 50 checks.

questions.onCorrect: In the worst case every item is checked once, so the checks equal the list's length.

misconceptions.feedback: The last item still has to be checked, so count it.
Half is an average guess. The worst case is the most checks any target could need.

questions.prompt: Indexes in a list start at 0. What is the index of the fourth item?
hints: Zero-based indexing labels the first item 0.
Write the indexes for the first four positions.
An item's index is one less than its ordinary position.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The indexes run 0, 1, 2, 3, so the fourth item has index 3.

questions.onCorrect: The first item is at index 0, so the fourth is at index 3: one less than its position.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the position, not the index. Indexes start counting from 0.

questions.prompt: Search the list in the figure for 17. How many comparisons does binary search make?
hints: Start with the middle of the seven sorted items.
Is the middle value too small or too large for 17, and which half does that rule out?
The comparison that finds the target counts too.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: First compare 11 at index 3, then 17 at index 5: two comparisons.

questions.onCorrect: The first middle rules out half the list, so the second comparison lands on the target.

misconceptions.feedback: The first middle is 11, not 17. The search needs another comparison.
That is how many checks a linear search would need. Binary search discards half after each comparison.

questions.prompt: Binary search looks for 11 in the sorted list in the figure. How many comparisons does it take?
hints: Find the middle item of the whole list before discarding anything.
The list has seven items, so the middle one is at index 3.
Compare what you find there with the target.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first middle value is 11, so the first comparison succeeds.

questions.onCorrect: If the first middle is the target, no halving is needed, and one comparison is the fewest a search can make.

misconceptions.feedback: Halving only follows a mismatch. Does the first middle match the target?
The search stops at the first match, so later halves are never needed.

questions.prompt: Search the list in the figure for 10. How many comparisons does it take to show that 10 is missing?
hints: Keep only the half that could still contain 10.
After each comparison, list the items that remain and take the middle of those.
Stop counting when no item is left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The compared values are 11, 5 and 8: three comparisons.

questions.onCorrect: Each comparison halved the range until it was empty, so showing that 10 is missing took only three.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a linear search, which checks every item. Binary search discards half each time.
After that many comparisons one item still remains, and it has to be compared.

questions.prompt: Search the list in the figure for 22, taking the lower middle each time. How many comparisons does it take?
hints: Use the lower middle whenever the remaining range has an even number of items.
After each comparison, write down which items are still possible.
Count every comparison, including the one that finds the target.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The search compares 10, 16, 19 and 22: four comparisons.

questions.onCorrect: Each comparison halves the range, so even a last-place target needs far fewer comparisons than the list has items.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a linear search. Binary search discards half after each comparison.
The search still has to compare the last remaining item. Count that one too.

questions.prompt: What can happen if binary search is run on a list that is not sorted?

courseChecks.description: Six problems about instructions and searches. Trace each case, then see which lessons will help.

question.prompt: What is x after the last assignment?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The assignments store 6, then 10, then 30. Multiplication uses the value stored by the preceding line.

question.prompt: Which value is stored in x when this program ends?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 < 12 is false. Only the else branch runs, storing 12 + 3 = 15.

question.prompt: After all five iterations, what is x?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: range(5) produces five iterations. Starting from 1 and adding 3 five times gives 16.

question.prompt: Linear search starts at the left and stops at its first match. How many value checks find 8?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It inspects 14, 6, 2, 19 and then 8. The target has index 4, but finding it takes 5 value checks.

question.prompt: Using the lower middle each time, how many value checks does binary search need to find 31?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The inspected values are 14, then 24, then 31. After each mismatch, the sorted order rules out the lower half.

question.prompt: For 63 already-sorted items with direct access, what is the worst-case number of binary-search value checks?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At most 6 value checks are needed: floor(log₂ 63) + 1 = 6. Sorting and access costs are excluded by the question.

question.prompt: How many times is the while condition tested, including the final false test?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The condition is tested at x = 11, 8, 5 and 2. The first three tests run the body; the fourth is false.

question.prompt: The first value is overwritten. What is the final x?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second line replaces 13 with 4. The remaining assignments store 20 and then 14.

acceptedIdeas: Linear search: 20 total
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Linear search uses 0 + 20 = 20 comparisons. Sorting then searching uses 50 + 5 = 55; the small lookup count excludes its preparation.

question.prompt: This rule should double x when its starting value is at least 10. Which replacement fixes the comparison?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: x >= 10 includes the boundary and every larger value. Equality alone would fail for values above 10.

question.prompt: How many value checks does a full linear search need to establish that 9 is absent?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: None of the six entries is 9. With no ordering shortcut, the search must check all six.

question.prompt: Use the lower middle and stop when the candidate interval is empty. How many checks establish that 20 is absent?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The search checks 13, 22, 16 and 19. No candidates remain between 19 and 22, so it reports absence after four checks.
